creator: Stefan Georgi
title: Secret of the DTC Universe #6: Avatar research is overrated
summary: An argument against building elaborate demographic/psychographic avatar profiles before writing ads. The creator's position is that the sub-segments people carve out of a market (divorced vs. married, empty nester vs. working mom, by ethnicity) share far more than they differ, so 90% of effort should go to the 'shared center' of the total addressable market — the common symptom cluster and life situation nearly every buyer in the category is living. He frames avatar research as a productivity illusion that delays the only thing that produces information (running ads with real money behind them), argues that specificity still belongs in the ad content itself (problem, outcome, mechanism, prior failure, believable detail) rather than in a segmentation database, and adds two caveats: it is fine to pursue genuinely different demographics once you have hit real scale and growth on the existing channel is getting hard, and when you do want to speak to a segment, a single situational opening line does the job that a four-week avatar project was supposed to do.
recencySignals: No explicit dates. Era cues: LLMs discussed as an everyday copy tool ('especially in the days of AI', 'trained on pretty much the entire corpus of human knowledge including a LOT of Reddit threads'), Meta named as the primary scaling channel, references to the author's own RMBC Method. Places it firmly in the post-ChatGPT era, roughly 2023 or later. Content is positioning/copy-strategy (durable class), so the imprecise date does not matter much.

tactics.claim: Write to the shared center of your total addressable market — the symptom cluster and life situation nearly every buyer in the category has in common — and put roughly 90% of your messaging effort there instead of building separate avatar profiles for each demographic slice.
tactics.mechanism: The sub-segments people carve out of a market have far more in common than not: a 52-year-old gut-supplement buyer is dealing with menopause, lower energy, and the same bloating/sleep/mood cluster regardless of marital status, ethnicity, or employment. That overlap is where the volume of the market sits, so copy aimed at it reaches nearly everyone, while copy aimed at a slice reaches a fraction and costs weeks of research to produce.
tactics.evidence: Worked illustration only: a 52-year-old female gut-supplement buyer enumerated across marital status, children, ethnicity and employment, with the shared attributes and shared symptom list listed out. No test, no account data, no comparison against a segmented approach.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (positioning and audience scoping), so age is irrelevant. It is an unusually good fit because natural deodorant has an exceptionally tight shared center: essentially every buyer is someone who wants off aluminium, has a two-week transition to survive, and has had a previous natural deodorant quit by noon or burn with baking soda — that cluster is already enumerated by marketing-problem-solution-inventory and the voice-of-customer agent. A solo operator at ~$2,700/mo with 12 SKUs, one $30/day campaign and a sub-1,000 list has no business generating segmented avatar briefs; the shared center is close to the whole market they can reach. Free, editorial, applies to PDP hero copy, Amazon bullets, A+ blocks and the Meta primary text going live now. Held at 7 rather than higher because it needs an explicit reconciliation with the one-narrow-persona-per-asset rule already recorded in marketing-product-image-stack: the resolution is that a single asset still speaks to one narrowly-stated person, but that person is drawn from the shared center's attributes (the buyer whose last natural deodorant quit by noon) rather than from a demographic segment — and because the evidence is a single hypothetical.

targetSkill.name: marketing-awareness-level-messaging
targetSkill.description: Use when deciding what a product page, Amazon listing, email or ad should actually say and who it should speak to — mapping copy to the reader's awareness level and the category's sophistication, and deciding how narrowly to segment the audience before writing (write to the shared centre of the market rather than building separate demographic avatar profiles).

tactics.claim: Cap the research phase and get assets in front of the market instead — deep avatar research produces the illusion of productivity while delaying the only thing that returns real information.
tactics.mechanism: Research feels like work and generates artefacts, but nothing in it is validated. Only putting copy in front of buyers with money behind it tells you whether the angle is right, so every additional week of profiling is a week of unvalidated guesses accumulating. The people who most enjoy building the research system are usually the ones avoiding the exposure of shipping.
tactics.evidence: Assertion, delivered as a personality read ('most of the people who love AvatarMaxxing are actually just using it as a cope for not taking action'). No data, no example of a research project that failed to pay off.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (effort allocation), age irrelevant, and it lands on a real live temptation: a Meta campaign is being stood up this week, and the alternative to writing two primary texts is another week of persona work. The grounding here is specific — `agents/voice-of-customer` already mines Reddit and Judge.me monthly into data/context/voice-of-customer.md, and personas.json already exists, so the marginal return on additional audience research is close to zero while the post-entry email sequence and the giveaway creative are unwritten. Capped at 5 because it is largely a restatement of the binding-constraint rule already at the top of marketing-performance-pattern-analysis (name what is actually capping output before doing more analysis), the evidence is pure assertion with an ad-hominem attached, and it protects hours rather than producing revenue. The additive part is narrow: it names audience research specifically as the activity most likely to masquerade as progress.

targetSkill.name: marketing-performance-pattern-analysis
targetSkill.description: Use when deciding where to spend the next block of marketing hours or diagnosing why results are flat — naming the binding constraint before critiquing assets, capping research and audience-profiling work that is not the constraint, tagging assets with their attributes at production time, and contrasting top and bottom performers to isolate the variable doing the work.

tactics.claim: Differentiate your creative on angle — one ad about the physical symptom, one about appearance, one about confidence, one about the frustration of a body that changed — rather than producing a separate ad per demographic avatar; all of them still hit the same shared centre.
tactics.mechanism: Different pain points inside one market catch different people at different moments without needing a different audience definition behind each ad, so you get real creative diversity from four angles against one audience instead of four near-identical ads against four thin segments. Splitting by demographic instead multiplies production work while the underlying message barely changes.
tactics.evidence: Illustrative list of four gut-supplement angles (menopause, appearance, confidence, body-change frustration) asserted to all speak to the market's centre. No performance figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (creative differentiation axis), so age is not the limiter, and it is directly actionable on the campaign going live: the 3-2-2 flexible ad needs three creatives and two meaningfully different primary texts, and this specifies what 'meaningfully different' should mean — different pain angle against the same buyer (transition-period fear, baking-soda irritation, the mid-afternoon shirt check, aluminium avoidance), not different demographic. That is exactly the shape a solo operator with no designer can actually produce, because the angles are already enumerated in marketing-problem-solution-inventory and the review corpus. Held at 6 because it substantially reinforces rules already recorded — 'cover distinct creative jobs rather than creative volume' and the concept-and-hook allocation rule — so the additive claim is narrow (the axis of difference is angle, not audience), and at ~54 orders/month and one flexible ad judged as a single unit, the choice will be made by judgement rather than measured.

targetSkill.name: marketing-paid-creative-testing
targetSkill.description: Use when choosing what goes into the creative slots of a small-budget Meta campaign and how the variants should differ — differentiating on pain angle rather than on demographic segment, covering distinct creative jobs instead of creative volume, building a 3-2-2 flexible ad, and deciding when a new angle or audience is allowed to be opened at all.

tactics.claim: Keep the specificity inside the ad itself — be specific about the problem, the desired outcome, the mechanism, the reason the buyer has struggled before, and the details that make the product believable — even when you skip avatar research entirely.
tactics.mechanism: Skipping segmentation research does not mean writing generically; the specificity that persuades lives in the content of the claim rather than in the demographic definition of who is reading it, so all five of these can be sharp while the audience definition stays broad.
tactics.evidence: A five-item list, asserted. No examples, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class, but every item on the list is already owned and better developed elsewhere in the library: exact-number specificity and the prior-attempt walkthrough ('the reason the person has struggled before') are both recorded in marketing-conversion-copy-angles, the named mechanism and where to find it are recorded in marketing-awareness-level-messaging, and the believable-detail rule (keep the irrelevant identifying detail on borrowed proof) is in both conversion-copy-angles and marketing-review-mining. Adopting a five-item restatement would add a near-duplicate entry whose only distinguishing feature is that it sits in a list, and duplicate coverage degrades skill triggering.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplication — all five specificity dimensions are already covered, with more mechanism and worked detail, by marketing-conversion-copy-angles (hard numbers, prior-attempt walkthrough, identifying detail on proof) and marketing-awareness-level-messaging (named mechanism, where to find the differentiator). Restating them as a checklist would degrade triggering accuracy without adding a mechanism.

tactics.claim: Do not open up a genuinely different demographic or market until you have reached real scale on the current one and further growth on your existing traffic channel has clearly become hard.
tactics.mechanism: A new demographic is a new research project, a new set of creative, and a split of the same budget — all justified only when the existing audience is close to exhausted. Before that point, the incremental buyer inside the current market is cheaper to reach than the first buyer in a new one.
tactics.evidence: Hypothetical: a gut-supplement brand doing nine figures on Meta to 50+ women deciding to go after 50+ men, where the creator concedes proper research would be essential. No data on where the threshold actually sits.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (audience expansion order), age irrelevant, and it has an honest scaled-down form that is runnable today rather than needing a park. Scale-down: at $30/day driving giveaway entries there is one campaign, one ad set and one flexible ad, so a second demographic cell would split ~84 modelled weekly entries below the level where the learning phase can exit at all — the rule today reads as 'do not open a men's angle, a teen angle or a new age bracket; every creative slot stays pointed at the core buyer until cost per entry stops improving with the existing audience'. That also lines up with the standing read that retention, not new audiences, is the binding constraint. Held at 6 because it is a decision not to act rather than a revenue mechanism, it overlaps the doom-cycle and restraint rules already recorded in marketing-paid-creative-testing and marketing-paid-media-measurement, and the source's own threshold (nine figures) is so far from this business that only the direction transfers. The genuine expansion version — researching and building for a new demographic — is what waits for scale.

targetSkill.description: Use when choosing what goes into the creative slots of a small-budget Meta campaign and how the variants should differ — differentiating on pain angle rather than on demographic segment, covering distinct creative jobs instead of creative volume, building a 3-2-2 flexible ad, and deciding when a new angle or audience is allowed to be opened at all.

tactics.claim: When you do want to speak to a specific segment, write one situational opening line for it and keep everything else the same — an LLM can supply that line, because it was trained on the forums the avatar research would have mined anyway.
tactics.mechanism: Segment specificity that actually registers with a reader is carried by a single recognisable situational sentence ('I'm still in great shape even though I'm in my 50s, which is why I don't understand what's going on in my gut'), not by a psychographic dossier. Since an ad is only one to four minutes of reading, one line is the entire budget the segment framing has; and a model trained on the relevant forum discourse can produce that line in seconds, so the research step that used to precede it is redundant.
tactics.evidence: Two hypothetical opening lines written live for 'fit dad in his 50s' and 'out-of-shape retiree', offered as proof that the whole job takes seconds rather than four weeks. Assertion plus a self-authored demonstration; no performance comparison against a researched version.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class in its core claim (segment framing is one sentence, not a dossier), though the 'LLMs already know it' half is a fast-moving capability claim worth re-checking rather than trusting. Genuinely usable and free here: the honest situational lines for this catalogue are already sitting in the review corpus — 'I work twelve-hour shifts', 'baking soda burns my skin', 'I sweat more than most people' — and each can open an email subject line, a Meta primary text or a PDP section while the body copy, mechanism and offer stay fixed. Capped at 5 because it substantially overlaps the re-entry rule already in marketing-awareness-level-messaging (hold the proven angle fixed and change only the entry point); the additive part is only that the varied entry point can be a *situation* as well as an awareness level. Also worth stating plainly: at ~54 orders/month and a sub-1,000 list, no segment line here will ever be measurably better than another, so this is a cheap way to widen coverage, not a test — and any situational line must reflect something a real reviewer said rather than an invented persona detail.
